def: Covariance divided by the product of the two standard deviations, between −1 and +1. Measures how well a straight line describes how two variables move together; says nothing about why.
A variable that causes both the treatment and the outcome, creating an association between them that is not the treatment's effect. Temperature for ice cream sales and drownings.
An association read in the wrong causal direction: the outcome causes the supposed cause, as wind turns windmills.
Distortion from analysing only units that passed a filter related to the variables of interest, so the analysed set differs systematically from the population.
A variable caused by two others, \(X \rightarrow C \leftarrow Y\). Conditioning on it (filtering, stratifying, adding it as a control) creates a spurious association between X and Y.
A spurious negative association produced by selecting on a collider, such as food and location quality among surviving restaurants (Berkson 1946).
A trend that holds in every subgroup reverses or vanishes when the subgroups are pooled, because the groups being compared have different subgroup mixes.
Comparing groups by applying each group's subgroup rates to one shared reference mix, so differences in mix no longer drive the comparison.
Directed acyclic graph: nodes for variables, arrows from cause to effect, no loops. Used to decide which variables to adjust for.
A path between treatment X and outcome Y that starts with an arrow pointing into X. Open back-door paths carry non-causal association and must be blocked by adjustment.
A set Z identifies the causal effect of X on Y if no member of Z descends from X and Z blocks every back-door path; then \(P(y\mid do(x))=\sum_z P(y\mid x,z)P(z)\).
A variable on the causal path from treatment to outcome (\(X \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y\)). Controlling for it removes the part of the effect that flows through it.
Graphical rule for whether a set of variables blocks every path between two nodes: chains and forks are blocked by conditioning on the middle, colliders are opened by it.
\(do(X{=}x)\) denotes setting X by intervention rather than observing it; \(P(y\mid do(x))\) is the causal quantity a randomized experiment estimates.
Ordering of causal evidence from anecdote, raw correlation and adjusted comparison through natural experiments to randomized and replicated experiments.
Quasi-experimental estimate: the treated group's before–after change minus the control group's, valid if both would have trended in parallel without treatment.
The list or mechanism from which a sample is actually drawn, such as an email list or a log table. Anyone outside it has zero chance of selection.
Bias from a sampling frame that omits part of the population, such as an email poll missing everyone without email.
Bias that arises when sampled units that do not respond differ on the outcome from those that do.
Bias from letting units choose whether to take part, as in opt-in polls, app-store reviews and thumbs feedback.
Drawing conclusions only from units that survived a filter, such as bombers that returned or users still active, while ignoring those that did not.
A sample of whoever is easiest to reach, such as a team's own prompts or nearby colleagues. Its inclusion probabilities are unknown.
Bias from sampling an atypical period, such as launch week, a holiday or one time zone's office hours.
Sampling units that are active at a random moment, which picks long-lived units (long sessions, slow jobs) in proportion to their duration.
Any design in which every population unit has a known, positive chance of selection, which makes unbiased estimates and honest error bars possible.
Dividing the population into groups (strata) and sampling at random within each, guaranteeing every group is represented and usually reducing variance.
Sampling whole groups (streets, conversations, repositories) and measuring every unit inside them. Cheaper, but variance is inflated by the design effect \(1+(m-1)\rho\).
Taking every k-th unit from an ordered list after a random start. Fails when the list has a period matching k.
Stratified allocation with stratum sample sizes proportional to stratum size times stratum standard deviation, which minimises variance for a fixed total n.
Reweighting respondents so each group's share matches its known population share. Fixes bias from the wrong group mix but not bias within groups.
Iterative proportional fitting of weights to match several known population margins in turn, used when their joint distribution is unknown.
Fits a multilevel model of the outcome by demographic cell, then weights cell predictions by population counts. Rescued the heavily skewed Xbox poll of 2012 (Wang et al. 2015).
\((\sum w_i)^2/\sum w_i^2\): the number of unweighted random observations with the same precision as a weighted sample.
Unbiased estimator of a population total that weights each sampled unit by the inverse of its inclusion probability.
Meng's \(\rho_{R,G}\): the correlation between being recorded and the value measured. The sample mean's error equals \(\rho\sqrt{(1-f)/f}\,\sigma\), so a tiny \(\rho\) ruins huge samples (Meng 2018).
The larger a non-random dataset, the more confidently wrong its estimates: error bars shrink with n while bias set by the data defect correlation does not.
